title: Ambrose and the emperor
hook: after a massacre, Ambrose makes the emperor do public penance

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambrose, made bishop by a shouting crowd before he was even baptized. Your line was chosen before ready.

A letter, written by hand, meant for one reader. The reader is the emperor Theodosius, a Christian, and a man who comes to church in Milan. The writer is the bishop of Milan, Ambrose. Something terrible has happened in the city of Thessalonica. After a riot there, the emperor's soldiers turned on the people of the city and killed them. The emperor is expected at Mass as usual. And the bishop has to decide what to say to him.
screen: `A LETTER FOR ONE READER.` → `A MASSACRE IN THESSALONICA.` → `THE EMPEROR EXPECTS MASS AS USUAL.`

segments.voice: Ambrose's letter is quieter than the legend. He doesn't denounce the emperor from the pulpit. He writes privately, and he writes as a pastor. He grieves over Thessalonica. He tells Theodosius plainly that he dare not offer the sacrifice of the Mass if the emperor intends to be there, not with this on his hands. And he points him to someone the emperor would know from scripture: King David. After David sent a man to his death, the prophet Nathan confronted him, and David didn't argue. In the Douay-Rheims: "And David said to Nathan: I have sinned against the Lord." Ambrose's message, more or less: a king did this before you. You can do it too. And Theodosius did. Ambrose describes it later, in the sermon he preached at the emperor's funeral. The emperor laid aside the signs of his royal rank, wept for his sin openly in church, and asked for pardon. Public penance, done by an emperor. Here's where the story grows. A later historian, Theodoret, tells a more dramatic version: Ambrose meets the emperor at the church door and blocks his way in front of everyone. Ambrose's own letter is private and patient. Both versions agree on the ending, though. The emperor stood among sinners and asked for mercy.
screen: `A PRIVATE LETTER, NOT A PUBLIC FIGHT.` · `DAVID: I HAVE SINNED.` · `THE EMPEROR LAYS ASIDE HIS RANK.` · `THE STORY GROWS IN THE RETELLING.` · then, large: `EVEN THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Think of someone with more power than you who needs to hear something true: a manager, an official, a landlord, someone older in the family. Shape the one sentence you'd say, with the anger taken out and the truth kept in, and notice Ambrose's way: privately first, with respect, leaving room to change. If you pray, pray for that person by name.
paenitentia. Latin for penance, what Ambrose asked of Theodosius after the massacre at Thessalonica, before the emperor could return to Mass. Today's word.
Your line: even the emperor. Nobody stands too high to ask for mercy. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics confess serious sin in the sacrament of penance, also called reconciliation; public penance like the emperor's belongs to the early Church, and today the sacrament is ordinarily private, between penitent and priest.

chat.says: Didn't a bishop once block an emperor at the church door?
options: That's a later telling; Ambrose's own letter was private, and the emperor did penance.
Yes, and Ambrose cut him off for life; the emperor never came back to Mass.
No, that's only a legend; the emperor never did any penance for Thessalonica.
chat.meaning: Ambrose wrote privately that he dare not offer Mass with Theodosius present; the emperor laid aside his rank and did public penance. The church-door scene is Theodoret's later version.

notes: 2 Kings 12:13 Douay-Rheims (Challoner): confirm the exact wording 'And David said to Nathan: I have sinned against the Lord.'

Ambrose, Letter 51 (Maurist numbering; Extra coll. 11) paraphrased: grief over Thessalonica; he dare not offer the sacrifice if the emperor intends to be present; the example of David; written in his own hand for the emperor alone. Confirm, especially the 'own hand' detail used in the hook.
On the Death of Theodosius 34 paraphrased: the emperor stripped off the royal insignia, wept publicly for his sin in church and sought pardon. Confirm section number.

Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History 5.17–18: the church-door confrontation; presented as a later, more dramatic account. Hook says only that soldiers killed the people of the city after a riot; no numbers or dates given, per the claims rule.
howItsDone: confirm the wording on public versus private penance.
